definition: The AI bubble is a concept that asserts there is a stock market bubble growing since 2025 amid the AI boom, a period of rapid increase in investment in artificial intelligence (AI) that is affecting the broader economy.
details: Speculation about a bubble largely originates from concerns that leading AI tech firms are involved in a circular flow of investments that are artificially inflating the value of their stocks. Some, like Ray Dalio, see similarities with the dot-com bubble of the 1990s and 2000s.

explainer.lead: The AI bubble is the claim that excitement and enormous investment have pushed some AI-related company values beyond what their profits and underlying businesses can justify. It matters because a sharp fall could affect not only technology firms, but also stock indexes, lenders, data-centre projects and the wider economy.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several lemonade-stand owners investing in one another and buying supplies from one another, making every stand look more valuable even though few customers are buying lemonade. People calling this an AI bubble worry that something similar is happening with AI companies, chips and data centres. That does not mean AI is useless; it means the prices and spending may have run ahead of the money the businesses can sustainably earn.
tiers.practitioner: For engineering and infrastructure decisions, treat bubble risk as a planning constraint rather than a prediction of a crash date. Stress-test GPU, cloud and data-centre commitments against lower demand, higher financing costs and slower revenue growth, while examining whether suppliers, customers and investors depend on one another. Useful products and genuinely improving models can still coexist with unprofitable deployments and overvalued companies.
tiers.paperLevel: The concept asserts that AI-related asset valuations and investment exceed levels supportable by market fundamentals, particularly monetization, profits and returns on infrastructure spending. Proposed mechanisms include circular financing, debt-funded data-centre construction, extreme index concentration and expectations that outpace measured productivity gains. These observations do not establish when or whether a correction will occur, and weak returns for individual firms do not imply that AI technology as a whole lacks value.

explainer.example: In September 2025, Nvidia announced a $100 billion investment in OpenAI, on the expectation that OpenAI would build additional data centres using Nvidia GPUs. Critics cite this as circular financing: the chip supplier funds a customer whose resulting hardware purchases can support the supplier’s own revenue and valuation.

usedIn.name: Equity market analysis
usedIn.detail: Used to examine stretched valuations and the concentration of major stock indexes in a few AI-linked companies.

usedIn.name: Credit and infrastructure finance
usedIn.detail: Used to assess risks in bonds, private credit and off-balance-sheet financing for AI data centres.

usedIn.name: Technology investment planning
usedIn.detail: Used to question whether chip and computing-capacity commitments are supported by durable revenue and productivity gains.

explainer.intuition: A bubble concern arises when rising prices attract more investment, and that investment helps push prices higher still, even without matching growth in profits. In AI, mutual investments and purchases among a small group of firms can make this loop especially hard to distinguish from healthy growth.
howItWorks: Expectations of future AI profits drive heavy spending and rising share prices.
AI firms, chip suppliers and partners invest in and buy from one another.
Debt and private credit expand the construction of computing infrastructure.
Weak near-term returns raise doubts about whether valuations are sustainable.
Falling confidence could reverse the loop through lower spending and asset prices.
explainer.whyItMatters: The scale and concentration of AI investment mean that a correction could reach beyond individual start-ups into broad retirement and investment portfolios. Debt-funded construction also creates the possibility of credit losses and unfinished or underused infrastructure if expected demand and profits fail to arrive.
misconceptions: Calling it a bubble does not mean AI is fake or has no useful applications.
Circular deals are evidence for concern, not proof that every AI company is overvalued.
High spending and rapid revenue growth do not by themselves demonstrate profitability.
The concept does not provide a reliable date for a market crash.
